title: the Markandeya
tomorrow: why can't two betrayed men stop worrying about who betrayed them?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vishnu Purana's last book: Vyasa in the river, calling the hardest age excellent because a sung name is enough. Today, a new Purana, and a king who would rather lose everything than take back his word.
screen: `THE HARD AGE HAS THE LOW DOOR.`

segments.voice: Somebody in a group chat promised to drive everyone to the concert. Now the car's dead and the only other one belongs to their mom, who needs it. Do they keep the promise whatever it costs, or call it off? A small version of a very old argument. In the Markandeya Purana, a king named Harishchandra promises the sage Vishvamitra a gift, and the sage asks for everything. Harishchandra keeps the promise. All of it. Readers have argued about him ever since.
screen: `THE CAR IS DEAD. THE PROMISE ISN'T.` → `A GIFT, AND THE SAGE ASKS FOR ALL.` → `HE KEEPS IT. ALL OF IT.`

segments.voice: This Purana carries the name of the sage Markandeya, who passes its answers along, and Harishchandra's story is one of them. The king hands over his kingdom. The sage demands a further fee. To pay it, Harishchandra sells his wife Shaibya and their son Rohita into service, then sells himself to the keeper of a cremation ground. One day a grieving mother brings a boy who died of a snakebite. It's Shaibya, with Rohita. Even then the king asks for the fee his master is owed. Then the gods appear, the boy lives, and all is restored. Now the two views. The first: truth is the ground everything stands on, and a king's word that can be bargained down isn't a word. Harishchandra doesn't make others pay to save himself; he pays first, and most, and at the end the gods themselves come to honor him. The second view is in the Purana too. In the next chapter, the sage Vasishtha, the king's family priest, hears what was done and is furious at Vishvamitra. The two sages curse each other into enormous birds and fight. Some readers hear in that rage the text admitting the cost was real, and they keep asking about Shaibya and Rohita, who never made the promise. The Purana keeps both: the honored king, and the angry sage.
screen: `A KINGDOM, A FAMILY, HIMSELF.` · `VIEW ONE: TRUTH IS THE GROUND.` · `VIEW TWO: VASISHTHA'S ANGER.` · `WHO PAYS FOR A PROMISE?` · then, large: `THE PURANA KEEPS BOTH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one promise you've made that has started to feel heavy. Name what you hoped it would do, then what's in the way, then one honest next step, whether that's keeping it or talking to the person you made it to. Breathe slowly with that step until the bell.
The Markandeya. The Purana told in the sage Markandeya's name, and inside it, Harishchandra, the king who kept his word.
Your line: the Markandeya. An honored king and an angry sage, kept side by side. That's today.

howItsDone: Harishchandra's story is retold in Hindu homes, plays and films as a story about truthfulness; the Markandeya Purana, which tells it, is also the home of the Devi Mahatmya.

fork.setup: your friend says Harishchandra was simply a terrible father. what's the strongest case for the other side?
options: he didn't think about his family; kings didn't, back then.
his word was the ground he stood on, and he paid first and most himself.

fork.reveal: the truth view at its best: he never made others pay to spare himself. and the other view is in the text too: Vasishtha's anger.

original.note: Sanskrit: truth, what is real. Harishchandra's story is told as a story about satya.
